papers.title: Eight limit cycles in a three-dimensional competitive Lotka-Volterra system
papers.abstract: Gyllenberg and Yan conjectured that a three-dimensional competitive Lotka-Volterra system can have at least five limit cycles. We prove the conjecture by constructing a strictly competitive system in which eight distinct limit cycles coexist near a single positive equilibrium. For each $m=5,6,7,8$, we construct a weak focus of order $m$ and identify parameter directions on the Hopf hypersurface that allow us to vary the first $m-1$ focus quantities independently. We choose these quantities so that the drift of a scalar amplitude function alternates in sign on $m$ nested level curves, forcing a limit cycle between each consecutive pair. A perturbation transverse to the Hopf hypersurface creates one additional cycle inside the others. The one-turn displacement map shows that both local counts are sharp. For each $m$, we give a rigorous computer-assisted proof that an explicit rational interaction matrix yields at least $m$ distinct hyperbolic limit cycles. We thank GPT-6 Astra for helping us compare earlier constructions, identify the main obstacle to extending them, and develop the present approach.

papers.title: A high-dimensional perspective of assortative mating: definition, dynamics, and limiting results
papers.abstract: Assortative mating, or the systematic (dis)similarity of traits between mate pairs, has wide-ranging consequences. Chiefly, it modulates genetic variance in offspring due to the coupling of inherited trait-associated loci in parents. Over many generations, this buildup becomes appreciable at the trait level and may confound statistical genetics techniques, such as association analyses and heritability estimation. Theoretical characterisations of this effect are well-developed in the univariate case, where mates assort on a single trait pair. However, empirical studies increasingly show that assortment is not only multivariate, but high-dimensional, in that the correlation structure exhibited between mates cannot be represented by a single or few linear combinations of the constituent traits. In spite of this, the mathematical theory of assortment has not scaled with awareness of this fact. In this paper such a generalisation is developed. We begin by deriving sufficient conditions under which an estimator is invariant to assortment, followed by studying existence conditions and limiting behaviour of equilibria under assortment. Finally, univariate results involving trait heritability and consanguineal genetic correlation are generalised to the multivariate regime.

papers.title: Emergent self-inhibition governs the landscape of stable states in complex ecosystems
papers.abstract: Species-rich ecosystems often exhibit multiple stable states with distinct species compositions. Yet, the factors determining the likelihood of each state's occurrence remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize and explain the landscape of stable states in the random Generalized Lotka--Volterra (GLV) model, in which multistability is widespread. We focus on the regime of the model where interspecies interactions are predominantly competitive and nearly symmetric. We find that the same pool of species with random initial abundances can result in different stable states, whose likelihoods typically differ by orders of magnitude. A state's likelihood increases sharply with its total biomass, or inverse self-inhibition. We develop a simplified model to predict and explain this behavior, by coarse-graining ecological interactions so that each stable state behaves as a unit. In this setting, we can accurately predict the entire landscape of stable states using only two macroscopic properties: the biomass of each state and species diversity. Our analyses also provide insight into the biomass--likelihood relationship: High-biomass states have low self-inhibition and thus grow faster, outcompete others, and become much more likely. These results reveal emergent self-inhibition as a fundamental organizing principle for the attractor landscape of complex ecosystems---and provide a path to predict ecosystem outcomes without knowing microscopic interactions.

papers.title: Nutrient limitation drives Turing instabilities in cross-feeding microbial communities
papers.abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by metabolic interactions, often in the form of cross-feeding in which microbes exchange metabolites via diffusion through the environment. We show here that the diffusion of cross-fed metabolites generically leads to a Turing instability in resource-poor environments, driven by the feedback between local metabolite availability and cell growth. A coarse-grained model of community biomass identifies the few dimensionless parameters that control the instability, most notably the ratio of environmental energy supply to cellular maintenance costs. We find that the detailed topology of the metabolic interaction network can be coarse-grained into a single effective parameter to quantitatively characterise the instability. Beyond the onset of the instability, the community forms compact aggregates whose merger is prevented by a competition for shared resources. Overall, our results demonstrate how spatial structure can arise as an inevitable consequence of metabolic interactions in a microbial community.

papers.title: Introduced cases, spread of infection in a community and travel control measures
papers.abstract: Travel restrictions, border screening and quarantine were widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic to prevent or delay the spatial spread of SARS-CoV-2, yet their effectiveness varied greatly across jurisdictions. To investigate how the timing and combination of border control measures interact with pathogen introductions and local transmission, we formulate a coupled Exporter--Importer epidemic model in both deterministic (ordinary differential equations) and stochastic (continuous-time Markov chain and multitype branching process approximation) frameworks. The model distinguishes latently infected, detected infectious and undetected infectious individuals, and explicitly separates recently arrived travellers in an introduction layer from the destination community. We derive analytical expressions for the control and basic reproduction numbers, final epidemic sizes and probabilities of outbreak extinction, and complement them with stochastic simulations. We show that pre-departure screening in the Exporter alone cannot prevent outbreaks in an Importer community with reproduction number larger than unity because latently infected travellers cross borders undetected. Post-arrival quarantine and screening in the introduction layer, as well as travel interruptions, can substantially reduce the attack rate in the Importer, but only when implemented with high stringency and triggered early. Triggering border interventions based on local detections in the Importer almost always acts too late because silent introductions precede local case detection, whereas triggers informed by surveillance in the Exporter provide a wider window of action. Effective protection of the Importer ultimately requires combining proactive, Exporter-informed border measures with local public health interventions that keep the community reproduction number near or below one.

papers.title: Interactions with hidden traits induce diversification and conceal its origin
papers.abstract: Adaptive diversification is often inferred from a small number of measurable traits, even though evolutionary dynamics arise from many interacting phenotypic dimensions. Unmeasured traits may therefore do more than bias inference: through their interactions, they may determine whether diversification occurs at all. Here we develop a theory of the onset and attribution of adaptive diversification by partitioning phenotype space into focal and hidden sectors. Eliminating the hidden sector yields an exact effective operator. Coupling to hidden traits that are stabilizing in isolation can destabilize an otherwise stable phenotype and generate a diversifying composite mode: the interaction creates diversification rather than merely strengthening it. Conversely, when the hidden sector is itself diversifying, the focal traits diversify as a correlated response to a hidden-driven process: no effective description in the focal traits, not even the exact one obtained by eliminating the hidden sector, predicts the variation they display, and stabilizing the focal traits reduces it without removing it. These effects become strongest near the hidden sector's own threshold, so a weakly stabilized hidden trait can have a large effect even with modest coupling to the focal traits, and they can generate correlations between focal traits that have no direct interaction. Onset and observability are distinct: systems with the same leading eigenvalue can project very differently onto the measured traits, so the theory tracks both the full operator and the focal-hidden partition. Individual-based simulations recover the predicted threshold and variance law, coupling-induced trait splitting, and the reversal of induced correlations. Interactions with unmeasured traits can both create adaptive diversification and determine whether the diversification seen in measured phenotypes can be attributed to them.

papers.title: Big Tree Viewer: A high-performance browser-based phylogenetic tree viewer with agentic AI integration
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic trees represent evolutionary history visually, and the ability to display and explore them is a key function in research across biological disciplines. Very large gene and species trees are becoming common with the increasing availability of low cost DNA sequencing, creating performance and informativeness challenges for display software originally designed for phylogenies with a few hundred to a few thousand tips. We discuss these limitations and introduce a browser-based Big Tree Viewer (BTV) highly optimized for fast display and biologically informative exploration of phylogenetic trees containing even a million tips. BTV can automatically map binomial species names to the NCBI or Catalogue of Life taxonomies and display colored ribbons to indicate taxonomic groups for enhanced exploration. Even without taxonomic mapping, BTV automatically labels groups of neighboring tips that share the first word of their names, such as a genus or gene family name, providing readable large-scale landmarks when individual tip labels are too dense to read. BTV supports metadata display, visual customization, tanglegram-like tree comparisons, statistics, figure export, and multiple tree layouts, including a new spiral form to display enormously large trees. BTV is also designed to integrate with common agentic AI tools, allowing agents to display, style, annotate, and inspect trees at the user's request. The BTV web app is freely available at https://BigTreeViewer.net and runs entirely in the user's browser, with no data uploads to any central server. Desktop versions of the BTV app for macOS, Windows, and Linux are also provided for download.

papers.title: Fluctuating resource availability stabilizes coexistence beyond the oscillatory tragedy of the commons
papers.abstract: Fluctuations in ambient conditions such as temperature and humidity can alter the effective availability of a shared resource at a given abundance. Standard evolutionary games with environmental feedback treat the payoff matrix as a deterministic function of resource abundance, leaving open how fluctuations in availability affect the oscillatory tragedy of the commons. Using noise-corrected replicator dynamics and individual-based birth-death simulations, we show that zero-mean fluctuations in resource availability can stabilize an interior equilibrium and suppress coupled strategy-resource oscillations. We derive an analytical criterion, in terms of the payoff structure and feedback dynamics, for when increasing noise favors local stability. These findings identify environmental variability as a mechanism that can promote strategy coexistence and help maintain shared resources in systems prone to recurrent depletion.
